name: BUF634AIDR
title: 36 V, 210 MHz, 250 mA high-speed open-loop buffer
summary: BUF634A is a unity-gain, open-loop buffer that delivers 250 mA from supplies of ±2.25 V to ±18 V. A pin selects its speed: BW tied to V– gives 210 MHz at 8.5 mA quiescent, BW open gives 35 MHz at 1.5 mA, and a resistor sets anything between. Slew rate is 3750 V/µs in both modes. It has an internal output current limit and thermal shutdown, works alone or inside an op amp's loop, and comes in SOIC, HSOIC with thermal pad and 3 mm × 3 mm VSON with thermal pad.
key_figures: 35 MHz to 210 MHz, set by BW pin

pins.name: BW
pins.function: Sets the bandwidth. Tied straight to V– it gives wide-bandwidth mode; left open it gives low-quiescent-current mode; a resistor from it to V– picks a bandwidth in between.

pins.name: Thermal Pad
pins.function: Exposed pad under the DDA and DRB packages only (the D package has none). It is tied to V– inside and must sit at the V– potential outside; soldered to a heat-spreading plane it lowers the thermal resistance, and it may also be left unconnected at a higher thermal resistance.

circuits.title: Buffer connections
circuits.description: The buffer on its own as an open-loop follower. The source drives VIN through RS, which with the source impedance shapes the frequency response. A 10 µF capacitor bypasses V+ and a second capacitor bypasses V–. R1 between BW and V– is the optional bandwidth-setting part; shorting BW to V– instead gives the widest bandwidth. VO drives RL to ground.

parts.note: optional; BW may instead go straight to V– for wide bandwidth

notes: The same pin numbers apply to the D, DDA and DRB packages.

circuits.title: High-performance headphone driver
circuits.description: An OPA1656 sets a non-inverting gain of +2 with two 1 kΩ resistors, its feedback taken from the buffer's output so the buffer sits inside the op amp's loop. The input is AC-coupled through 1 µF, with 100 kΩ from the non-inverting input to ground. BW is tied to V– for wide-bandwidth mode, and the buffer drives headphones or a small speaker returned to ground.
notes: Supply connections of U2 are not specified.

circuits.title: ATE and test pin driver
circuits.description: An OPA2810 drives the buffer inside its loop to drive a large capacitive load such as many device-under-test inputs. RISO in series with the buffer's output isolates the load capacitance CL. RF runs from the far side of RISO back to the inverting input, and CF runs from the buffer's output to the same input. BW is tied to V– for wide-bandwidth mode.
notes: Values of RF, CF, RISO and CL are not specified; supply connections of U2 are not specified.

circuits.title: Pseudo-ground driver
circuits.description: Splits a single +24 V supply into ±12 V about a driven mid-rail. Two 10 kΩ resistors halve the rail and feed the buffer's input, and the buffer's output is the pseudo-ground. The buffer runs from +24 V and ground, with 10 µF across the +24 V supply. C2 and C3 are the system bypass capacitors from each rail to the pseudo-ground.
notes: +12 V lies across C2 and +12 V across C3, giving ±12 V about the pseudo-ground.
BW is not connected.

circuits.title: Current-output valve driver
circuits.description: A voltage-to-current driver for a valve coil. An OPA2810 drives the buffer, whose output pushes current through the valve into a 10 Ω sense resistor to ground. The voltage on the sense resistor returns to the op amp's inverting input, so the coil current follows the input: a ±2 V input gives ±200 mA.
notes: IO = ±200 mA through the valve.
Supply connections and the BW pin are not specified.

circuits.title: Bridge-connected motor driver
circuits.description: Two buffered op amps drive a motor between their outputs. One half of an OPA2810 is a non-inverting stage of gain 10 (1 kΩ to ground, 9 kΩ feedback) driving the first buffer; its output is one motor terminal. The other half inverts that terminal with two 10 kΩ resistors, its non-inverting input grounded, and drives the second buffer onto the other motor terminal. A ±1 V input gives ±20 V across the motor at 250 mA.
notes: ±20 V across the motor at 250 mA.
Supply connections and the BW pins are not specified.

circuits.title: Boosting op amp output current
circuits.description: The buffer sits inside the feedback loop of an OPA2810, which sets a gain of 2 V/V with a 1 kΩ input resistor to ground and a 1 kΩ feedback resistor from the buffer's output; the loop corrects the buffer's offset and other errors while the buffer supplies up to ±250 mA into RL. C1 (10 pF in the worked design) from the inverting input to the op amp's output is needed only with high-speed, unity-gain-stable op amps. BW may be tied to V– for wide-bandwidth mode where stability requires it. The worked design runs from ±12 V over –40°C to +125°C with a bandwidth above 100 kHz.

parts.note: optional; used with fast op amps that are stable at unity gain

notes: The BW-to-V– link sets wide-bandwidth mode and is fitted only if required.
Design targets: ±12 V supplies, –40°C to +125°C, gain 2 V/V, ±250 mA output, bandwidth above 100 kHz.
Supply connections of U2 are not specified.

operation.text: A unity-gain, open-loop complementary follower for high output current and high slew rate. It runs alone as a line or load driver, or inside an op amp's feedback loop, where the op amp sets precision and distortion and the buffer adds current, keeps the heat of the output stage away from the precision part and improves capacitive-load drive. Its 3750 V/µs slew rate adds little delay inside such a loop.

The –3 dB bandwidth into 1 kΩ is 210 MHz with BW shorted to V– and 35 MHz with BW floating; a resistor from BW to V– sets values between. Quiescent current scales with it, about 8.5 mA at 210 MHz and 1.5 mA at 35 MHz. For a given resistor the bandwidth also depends on the load resistance.

Continuous output is up to ±250 mA and an internal limit holds the output near ±350 mA. Asking for more swing than a load allows runs into that limit and the output stops being linear. Often heat, not the limit, caps the continuous current, and swing falls with junction temperature and current. In wide-bandwidth mode with high supply and heavy load, keep the junction below its maximum or the part can be damaged.

The output stage switches off near 180°C junction and current is limited while the die cools; it switches back on near 160°C. Supply current is about 12 mA while shut down. The on-off cycle can repeat with a period from under a second to minutes, set by package, signal, load and cooling. Tripping it in normal service means too little heat sinking or too much dissipation for the package.

Every pin has ESD diodes to both supplies; they tolerate about 10 mA continuous and give some protection against input overdrive past the rails. If the input can go beyond the supplies, add a series input resistor, kept small since a large one costs noise and bandwidth. VIN is not fail-safe: bring up V+ and V– before any signal reaches VIN, and keep any diode current below 10 mA.
With VIN left open the output can go to either supply, depending on which way the input bias current flows.

Source resistance changes high-frequency peaking, overshoot and ringing; a 25 Ω to 200 Ω series input resistor usually gives the best response, depending on the source. A 10 Ω to 150 Ω resistor in series with the output can improve the response into some loads, capacitive ones in particular. When driving many DUT inputs in automatic test equipment, an isolation resistor at the output keeps phase margin adequate.

For the composite loop to be stable the buffer must add little phase, roughly 20° or less at the op amp's unity-gain frequency for a G = +1 circuit. Most general-purpose and precision op amps stay unity-gain stable with the buffer inside; large capacitive loads may need wide-bandwidth mode, and fast or quick-settling op amps usually call for it. Check for oscillation or ringing on pulses with the real load and worst-case conditions. In the worked OPA2810 design, gain 2 V/V, feedback and input resistors are both 1 kΩ and C1 is 10 pF; THD+N in the loop beats the buffer alone because of the op amp's feedback, and with 16 Ω and 32 Ω loads distortion climbs at large output swing as the short-circuit limit acts.

Supply span is 4.5 V to 36 V (±2.25 V to ±18 V), single, split balanced or split unbalanced. Output swing shrinks at low supply such as ±2.25 V. On a single supply with V– at ground the DC error from the negative-supply rejection term is smallest.

Place a 0.1 µF high-frequency capacitor less than 0.1 in from each supply pin, with a larger capacitor, typically 10 µF, alongside. On a single supply only V+ gets them; on split supplies each rail gets them to ground. The larger capacitors may sit farther away and be shared by several parts nearby. As little as 0.1 µF keeps most circuits stable, but fast, heavy output current may call for 10 µF solid tantalum parts; for high-frequency open-loop work use a ground plane and 0.1 µF ceramic chip capacitors at the pins in parallel with 10 µF solid tantalum.

Thermal-pad packages have much lower thermal coefficients than the plain SOIC, given a board laid out to the thermal-pad guidelines; an unsoldered pad raises thermal impedance a great deal and can cause overheating. Count dynamic as well as quiescent dissipation; where the signal is irregular, an RMS estimate of dissipation shows whether there is a problem.

Put low-ESR 0.1 µF ceramic capacitors from each supply pin to ground as near the part as possible (only V+ on a single supply). Use a ground plane and keep analog and digital grounds apart, minding where ground current flows. Route inputs away from supply and output traces, crossing them at right angles if they must cross, and keep input traces short. Place the external parts close to the device. Clean the board after assembly; after aqueous cleaning, bake at 85°C for 30 minutes to drive out moisture. Solder the SOIC to the board rather than socketing it, since much of its heat leaves through the leads, and use wide traces on every pin, unconnected pins included.

Etch lands for the leads and the pad. Put 13 vias of 0.01 in (0.254 mm) diameter in the pad area, small enough that solder does not wick down them in reflow; further vias, larger if wished, can go anywhere on the thermal plane outside the pad. Tie the pad to V– and connect every pad via to the V– plane with a full ring, not thermal spokes. Leave the leads and the via-filled pad open in the top solder mask, and paste the pad and all leads before reflow.
Across 14000 devices the offset voltage has a mean of 35.7 mV and a standard deviation of 2.15 mV.
Three 8-pin packages: D (SOIC, 4.90 mm × 3.90 mm), DDA (HSOIC with thermal pad, 4.90 mm × 3.90 mm) and DRB (VSON with thermal pad, 3.00 mm × 3.00 mm). Rated for –40°C to +125°C.
